stem: PLACEHOLDER SAMPLE. A possessor has openly farmed a parcel for 12 years in a jurisdiction with a 20-year statutory period. The prior possessor, who farmed it for 10 years, sold his interest to the current possessor by deed. Which element is most directly satisfied by adding the two periods together?
explanation: Tacking lets successive possessors in privity combine their periods of possession to meet the continuity requirement for the statutory period.

stem: PLACEHOLDER SAMPLE. Two squatters occupied the same cabin, one after the other, with no transfer between them. The second squatter claims adverse possession by tacking. What is the best response?
choices: Tacking is allowed because the possession was continuous in fact
Tacking is not allowed because there was no privity between the possessors
Tacking is allowed only if the first squatter consents in writing
Tacking is not allowed because squatters can never adversely possess
Tacking is allowed because both possessors were hostile
explanation: Tacking requires privity, meaning a voluntary transfer of the possessory interest between successive possessors. Sequential unrelated squatters lack privity.

stem: PLACEHOLDER SAMPLE. Under the Wisconsin statute, what is the general period of adverse possession when the claimant has no color of title and pays no taxes?
explanation: Wis. Stat. § 893.25 sets a 20-year period for adverse possession not founded on a written instrument. (Placeholder: verify against the current statute.)

stem: PLACEHOLDER SAMPLE. A claimant admits in a court filing that the record owner holds title to the disputed strip but asks to keep using it. This admission most directly undermines which element?
explanation: Acknowledging the true owner's superior title is inconsistent with possession under a claim of right, so the hostility element fails (as in Van Valkenburgh v. Lutz).

stem: PLACEHOLDER SAMPLE. Which of the following is generally NOT subject to adverse possession?
choices: Farmland owned by an absentee landlord
A strip of a neighbor's yard
explanation: Government-owned land is generally exempt from adverse possession claims.
